title: The Room of Harrow Glen
premise: Quentin Thackeray, a hospice nurse at Harrow Glen, has spent years recording the strange habit the dying share: counting backwards from ten. When the house's mirrors begin showing the room one second behind reality, he realizes the counts were never deaths — they were invitations, and someone in the house has finally accepted. Trapped overnight during a winter storm with the dying resident Edmund Voss and a staff that may not be what it seems, Quentin must uncover which of them invited the room in before it finishes counting down to zero. In the end, Quentin chooses to take the invitation himself, trading his place in the world for Edmund's release — and the final chapter reveals his documentation, read by a new nurse, still counting.
about_author: Xanthe Iversen is the pen name of a former palliative care volunteer from coastal Maine who spent six years sitting with the dying and swears every word of her fiction is 'only slightly exaggerated.' She writes at night, in rooms without mirrors.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Introduces Harrow Glen hospice and Quentin's ritual of documenting the dying, who all count backwards from ten. He frames it as a private prayer, a professional quirk. Emotional beat: tender melancholy establishing his need to record everything as a way of holding grief at arm's length.

chapters.title: Ten, Nine, Eight
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A patient named Alma dies mid-count, but her lips keep moving for three seconds after her heart stops. Quentin writes it down, tells no one. Emotional beat: the first hairline crack in his rational worldview, dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: Harrow Glen in Winter
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Atmospheric portrait of the house: its history as a private sanatorium, the sealed east wing, the staff — head nurse Delphine, orderly Marcus, night aide Priya. Emotional beat: belonging; Quentin loves this strange place and its people, which raises the stakes for what follows.

chapters.title: The New Admission
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Edmund Voss, a wealthy, frightened old man, arrives insisting he is not dying and refusing to face any reflective surface. His family has paid for 'round-the-clock discretion.' Emotional beat: unease; Edmund's terror is specific, and he looks at Quentin like he recognizes him.

chapters.title: What the Mirrors Keep
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Edmund begs Quentin to cover the hallway mirror. Quentin humors him, then catches his own reflection smiling a half-beat after he does. Emotional beat: violation; the intimate instrument of self-regard becomes a stranger's face.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Prayer
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Flashback chapter to Quentin's first death vigil years ago, where he first heard a patient counting backwards and began his notebooks. Emotional beat: reveals his compulsion as grief-avoidance, deepening character before the horror escalates.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Every mirror in the house now lags by exactly one second. He tests them with a stopwatch, documents the discrepancy, and shows Delphine — who goes white and forbids him to speak of it. Emotional beat: isolation; the truth-teller is told to be quiet.

chapters.title: Delphine Knows
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Delphine privately inspects the east wing's sealed doors, checks a ledger of former residents, and murmurs 'not again.' She burns a page. Emotional beat: fear and complicity; the reader learns the house has a history of this.

chapters.title: The Storm Arrives
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. A blizzard seals the roads; the night shift is skeleton crew. Edmund's family calls to say they cannot reach him until morning. The phones die. Emotional beat: entrapment; the world shrinks to the house and its lagging reflections.

chapters.title: Marcus's Hands
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus, the orderly, moves through the halls without appearing in any mirror at all. He knows Quentin has noticed. A tense, almost friendly confrontation in the kitchen. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth — Marcus protects the house's secret out of love for Delphine.

chapters.title: Edmund's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Edmund admits he came to Harrow Glen deliberately: the house is a door, and the dying who count backwards are its congregation. He has spent his life fleeing it, and his money bought him a room at the threshold. Emotional beat: dread reframed as pilgrimage.

chapters.title: The Room Itself
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Edmund describes the Room: a space that exists one second behind the world, where the invited go when the count reaches zero. Everyone who has died at Harrow Glen is there, still counting, waiting for someone to finish the number. Emotional beat: cosmic horror rendered intimately.

chapters.title: Priya's Night
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya finds the east wing unsealed and wanders in, drawn by her mother's voice — a woman who died at Harrow Glen years ago. She returns changed, humming a countdown. Emotional beat: grief weaponized; the Room knows exactly what each person wants back.

chapters.title: The Ledger of the Invited
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin steals Delphine's ledger: every death at Harrow Glen since 1911, each marked with the number they reached before dying. None reached zero. The count is still running, cumulative, across a century. Emotional beat: vertigo; the countdown is one long unbroken ritual.

chapters.title: Delphine's Bargain
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Delphine confesses to Quentin: her sister died here, and Delphine has kept the house running, feeding it small deaths, to keep the count from reaching zero on her watch. Emotional beat: power's corruption — she has sacrificed strangers to protect her own grief.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Edmund reveals the truth: he accepted the invitation decades ago as a young man, desperate to reach his dead wife, and has been running from the completion of his own count ever since. The Room has been patient. Emotional beat: guilt as engine; Edmund is both victim and cause.

chapters.title: Reflections Without Owners
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The lag widens to two seconds. Quentin sees figures in the mirrors that aren't in the room — former residents, faces from the ledger. One of them is Alma. Emotional beat: the dead are not malevolent; they are waiting, which is worse.

chapters.title: Marcus Breaks
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus, torn between loyalty to Delphine and the truth, gives Quentin the east wing key and admits he has been mirrorless for years — the Room took his reflection as payment for sparing Priya's mother's soul, or so he was told. Emotional beat: loyalty cracking under the weight of truth.

chapters.title: The East Wing
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin and Edmund enter the sealed wing: the original Room, doorless now, its walls covered in tally marks — thousands of them, counting down from a number no one wrote at the top. Emotional beat: awe and terror; the house was built around the countdown, not the other way around.

chapters.title: Seven, Six, Five
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The tally marks begin erasing themselves. Edmund's count, dormant for sixty years, resumes. The mirrors throughout the house all show the same thing: the Room, empty, waiting. Emotional beat: acceleration; the horror becomes a deadline.

chapters.title: Priya Sings
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya, fully claimed, leads the count aloud through the halls. Staff and dying patients join without knowing why. Delphine tries to stop her and sees her sister's face in a window's reflection. Emotional beat: the house becomes a congregation; belonging turned monstrous.

chapters.title: The Choice of Delphine
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Delphine decides to finish the count herself, believing she can enter the Room and pull her sister out. Quentin argues the ledger proves no one has ever come back. She goes anyway. Emotional beat: love curdled into hubris; power's corruption complete.

chapters.title: What Delphine Found
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin follows and finds Delphine at the threshold, frozen mid-step, one second behind herself — visible in the mirror but no longer in the room. Her sister's voice calls from inside. Emotional beat: horror of the almost; she is neither here nor there.

chapters.title: Four, Three
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. The house itself begins lagging — sounds arrive after their causes, footsteps echo before steps. Edmund's body starts failing as his count nears its end. Emotional beat: reality losing the race with the Room; time is literally running out.

chapters.title: The Truth About Marcus
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus admits the full truth: there was no bargain. The Room simply doesn't want him — the unloved and unloving are invisible to it. His loyalty to Delphine was the only warmth he had, and he gave it up to help Quentin. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; belonging denied even by the monster.

chapters.title: Quentin's Notebooks
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin rereads his own documentation and finds entries he doesn't remember writing, in his handwriting, counting down. The Room has been using his compulsion — his prayer — as its instrument. Emotional beat: betrayal by the self; his identity as recorder is the trap.

chapters.title: Two
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund, dying in truth now, asks Quentin not to save him but to witness him — to write his real story, the invitation, the wife, the flight. Quentin documents everything, and the act becomes an actual prayer for the first time. Emotional beat: redemption through truth-telling; documentation as communion, not control.

chapters.title: The Wife in the Glass
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Edmund's dead wife appears in the mirror, one second behind, holding out her hand. Quentin realizes the Room's power is not malice but longing — it is made of everyone who couldn't stop reaching backwards. Emotional beat: pity for the monster; horror and grief become the same thing.

chapters.title: One
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. The count reaches one and holds. The house stands at the threshold, every mirror showing the Room, every resident frozen mid-breath. Edmund's hand hovers over the final tally. Emotional beat: suspended apocalypse; the whole novel holds its breath.

chapters.title: The Invitation Accepted
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin understands the only way to close the count: someone must finish it in Edmund's place, willingly, with full knowledge. He writes his final entry, addresses it to whoever finds it, and speaks the word 'zero.' Emotional beat: sacrifice as authorship; he ends the story by entering it.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV inside the threshold. Quentin crosses: the Room is his hospice ward, every patient he ever lost sitting up, mid-count, finally able to stop. Edmund's count dissolves; Edmund dies in peace, witnessed. Emotional beat: terrible grace; the afterlife as a waiting room finally emptied.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Dawn. The storm breaks. The mirrors show only the present, one second early if anything — eager now. Edmund is gone; Delphine is found standing in the east wing, aged, silent, her sister's name the only word she can say. Emotional beat: exhausted relief shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: After Harrow Glen
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya wakes with no memory of the night but an aversion to her own reflection. The house is quiet. The dying, when they come, simply die. Emotional beat: hollow normalcy; the survivors inherit a silence they cannot explain.

chapters.title: The Empty Notebook
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Delphine finds Quentin's final entry and his forty notebooks, reads them cover to cover, and understands everything Quentin understood too late. She decides to keep the house open — but honest now, with the ledger public and the east wing consecrated. Emotional beat: penance; power relinquished at last.

chapters.title: What Marcus Remembers
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus looks in a mirror for the first time in years and sees himself — Quentin's sacrifice returned his reflection, a gift he didn't ask for. He weeps, then packs his things. Emotional beat: grief as the price of being seen; belonging finally granted, too late to share.

chapters.title: The New Nurse
chapters.summary: New character POV: Rosa, a hospice nurse, arrives to interview at Harrow Glen. Delphine hires her with one condition: read the notebooks, all of them, before her first shift. Emotional beat: transmission; the story becomes the house's immune system.

chapters.title: The Room, One Second Late
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa reads through the night. In the hallway mirror, she sees the east wing door standing open behind her — it is closed in the room itself. One second late. Emotional beat: the dread returns, smaller and patient; nothing is ever finished.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. In the final notebook, Rosa finds a page in Quentin's handwriting dated tomorrow, addressed to her by name: 'If the count starts again, don't pray it away. Witness it.' Emotional beat: chill and comfort entwined; Quentin is still documenting, from the other side of the glass.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV, final chapter. Rosa takes the night shift. A dying patient begins to count backwards from ten, and Rosa — instead of looking away — takes his hand and counts with him. The mirrors hold steady. Emotional beat: resolution as transformation; the answer to the horror is presence, not control. The last line is the patient's whispered 'one.'

chapters.title: Zero (Coda)
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, one page, from the other side. Quentin, in the emptied Room that is now just light, writes the true final entry in a notebook that appears on Delphine's desk the next morning: 'It was never a countdown. It was a roll call. Everyone is accounted for.' Emotional beat: peace; the horror was longing, and the longing is answered.
